H.history:
In the 16th century Paracelsus noticed that metals dissolving in acids give off a gas, and in 1671 Robert Boyle described the same flammable gas from iron filings and dilute acid. Nobody realised it was a distinct substance until **Henry Cavendish** studied it carefully in **1766**. He called it “inflammable air”, measured its very low density, and later showed that burning it produces only water.

In 1783 Antoine Lavoisier repeated the experiment and named the gas *hydrogène*, from the Greek *hydro* (water) and *genes* (forming): the water-former. Hydrogen balloons followed within months (Jacques Charles, 1783). In the 20th century hydrogen-filled airships ended with the Hindenburg fire of 1937. Its heavy isotopes were found later: deuterium by Harold Urey in 1931 (Nobel Prize 1934) and tritium in 1934.
H.production:
About 95 % of today’s hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mainly by **steam–methane reforming**. Methane and steam react over a nickel catalyst at 700–1000 °C (CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂). The **water–gas shift reaction** then turns the carbon monoxide into more hydrogen (CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂). This releases a lot of CO₂, which is why “green” hydrogen made by electrolysis of water with renewable electricity is being developed. Hydrogen is also a by-product of the chlor-alkali process.

Roughly half of all hydrogen goes into **ammonia** for fertiliser (the Haber–Bosch process). Most of the rest is used in oil refineries to remove sulfur and to crack heavy oil, and to make methanol.
H.chemistry: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe (about 74 % of normal matter by mass), but on Earth it is almost all locked up in water and organic compounds. It can **lose** its electron to become H⁺ (the basis of acids), **gain** one to become the hydride ion H⁻ (with very reactive metals, as in NaH), or **share** it in covalent bonds. When H is bonded to N, O or F it takes part in **hydrogen bonding**, which explains the high boiling point of water and the structure of DNA. Its position on the periodic table is debated, because it behaves partly like group 1 and partly like group 17.

reactions.note: Combustion: very exothermic (ΔH = −286 kJ per mole of liquid water). The basis of hydrogen fuel cells and the ‘squeaky pop’ test.
The Haber–Bosch process: iron catalyst, about 450 °C and 200 atm.
A common way to make hydrogen in the laboratory.
Explodes in sunlight through a radical chain reaction.
With very reactive metals, hydrogen forms ionic hydrides containing H⁻.

H.safety: Hydrogen is **extremely flammable**. It burns in air at anywhere from 4 % to 75 % concentration, needs very little energy to ignite, and burns with an almost invisible flame in daylight. Its tiny molecules leak through fittings easily, and over time it can make some metals brittle. It is not toxic, but in a closed space it can displace oxygen.

He.history:
Helium was discovered **in the Sun before it was found on Earth**. During the solar eclipse of 18 August **1868**, the French astronomer **Jules Janssen** saw a bright yellow line at 587.49 nm in the spectrum of the solar prominences. It did not match the nearby sodium D lines. **Norman Lockyer** and **Edward Frankland** concluded that it came from an unknown element and named it after the Greek *helios*, the Sun.

For almost 30 years many chemists doubted it existed. Then in **1895 William Ramsay** treated the uranium mineral cleveite with acid and found that the gas released showed the same yellow line. Per Teodor Cleve and Nils Langlet in Uppsala found it independently in the same year and measured its atomic weight. In 1905 helium was found in natural gas from a well in Dexter, Kansas, which made large-scale production possible. In 1908 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied it at 4.2 K, opening the field of low-temperature physics.
He.production:
All of the helium on Earth is made by the **alpha decay of uranium and thorium** in rocks: an alpha particle is a helium nucleus. Over millions of years this helium collects in the same underground traps as natural gas, sometimes reaching several percent. It is extracted by **cooling the natural gas** until everything except helium liquefies. The main producers are the United States, Qatar, Algeria and Russia.

Once released into the air, helium is so light that it eventually escapes into space, so it is a **non-renewable resource** on human time-scales. The biggest uses are cooling the superconducting magnets in **MRI scanners**, leak detection, shielding gas for welding, breathing mixtures for deep diving, and balloons.
He.chemistry: Helium has a complete 1s² shell and the **highest first ionization energy** of any element (2372 kJ/mol), so it forms no stable compounds under ordinary conditions. Only exotic species exist: the HeH⁺ ion (detected in space in 2019) and Na₂He, which forms only at pressures above about 113 GPa. Helium is also the only element that **does not solidify at atmospheric pressure**, even at absolute zero. Below 2.17 K liquid helium-4 becomes a **superfluid** that flows without viscosity and creeps up the walls of its container.

reactions.note: Alpha decay: the source of almost all helium on Earth. Helium does not react chemically under normal conditions.
Nuclear fusion in the Sun (proton–proton chain) turns hydrogen into helium and releases the energy that powers stars.

He.safety: Helium is non-toxic and non-flammable, but it is an **asphyxiant**. Breathing pure helium (for example from a pressurised tank to make a squeaky voice) can cause loss of consciousness or death from lack of oxygen, or a gas embolism. Liquid helium at −269 °C causes severe cold burns, and as it boils into gas its volume grows about 750 times, which can burst sealed containers.

Li.history:
In **1817 Johan August Arfwedson**, working in Jöns Jacob Berzelius’s laboratory in Stockholm, analysed the mineral petalite from the island of Utö in Sweden. He found an alkali that was not sodium or potassium. Because it had been found in a mineral rather than in plant ashes, Berzelius named it after the Greek *lithos*, stone. Arfwedson could not isolate the metal. **William Thomas Brande** obtained a small amount in 1821 by electrolysing lithium oxide, and in 1855 **Robert Bunsen** and **Augustus Matthiessen** made larger quantities by electrolysing molten lithium chloride.

For a century lithium had few uses. In 1949 the Australian psychiatrist **John Cade** discovered that lithium salts calm mania, and lithium carbonate is still a major treatment for bipolar disorder. The invention of the **lithium-ion battery** (John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino, Nobel Prize 2019) made it one of the most strategic elements of the 21st century.
Li.production:
There are two main sources. In the salt flats (*salares*) of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia, the so-called “lithium triangle”, lithium-rich **brine** is pumped into huge evaporation ponds. After 12–18 months in the sun, lithium is precipitated as **lithium carbonate**. In Australia, the largest producer, the hard-rock mineral **spodumene** (LiAlSi₂O₆) is mined, roasted at about 1050 °C, and leached with sulfuric acid. China also processes much of the world’s lithium. The metal itself is made by electrolysing a molten mixture of LiCl and KCl.

Most lithium now goes into **batteries** for phones, laptops and electric vehicles. It is also used in heat-resistant glass and ceramics, lithium greases, aluminium–lithium alloys for aircraft, and medicine.
Li.chemistry: Lithium is the **lightest metal** (0.534 g/cm³: it floats on oil and water), and the least reactive alkali metal. Its tiny Li⁺ ion has a very high charge density, so lithium behaves somewhat like magnesium, the **diagonal relationship**. For example, it is the only alkali metal that reacts with nitrogen at room temperature (forming Li₃N), and its carbonate decomposes on heating like MgCO₃. Lithium has the most negative standard reduction potential of all elements (−3.04 V), which is why it makes such good high-voltage batteries.

reactions.note: Steady fizzing, much gentler than sodium or potassium.
Unique among the alkali metals: lithium slowly forms a dark nitride in air.
Burns with a crimson flame to form the normal oxide (sodium forms a peroxide, potassium a superoxide).
On strong heating, like group 2 carbonates and unlike the other group 1 carbonates.
In a lithium-ion battery, lithium ions move in and out of the graphite anode during discharge and charging.

Li.safety: Lithium metal reacts with water to give flammable hydrogen and corrosive lithium hydroxide. Lithium fires cannot be put out with water or CO₂: a class D powder or dry sand is needed. Damaged lithium-ion batteries can undergo **thermal runaway** and catch fire. Medical lithium has a narrow safe range, so patients need regular blood tests.

Be.history:
In **1798 Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin** showed that the gemstones beryl and emerald contain the oxide of a new element. Because its salts taste sweet, the element was first called *glucinium* (Greek *glykys*, sweet). This is a dangerous way to identify a chemical, since beryllium compounds are highly toxic. In **1828 Friedrich Wöhler** and **Antoine Bussy** independently isolated the metal by heating beryllium chloride with potassium. The name *beryllium*, from the mineral beryl, was officially adopted in 1949.

In 1932 James Chadwick discovered the **neutron** by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles: ⁹Be + ⁴He → ¹²C + n.
Be.production:
Beryllium is extracted from **bertrandite** (mined mainly in Utah, USA) and **beryl** (Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈). The ore is converted to beryllium hydroxide and then to beryllium fluoride, which is reduced with **magnesium** at about 1300 °C: BeF₂ + Mg → Be + MgF₂. World production is only a few hundred tonnes a year.

Beryllium is light, very stiff, and transparent to X-rays. It is used for **X-ray windows**, the gold-coated mirror segments of the **James Webb Space Telescope**, aerospace parts, and nuclear reactors (it reflects neutrons). **Beryllium–copper** alloy makes non-sparking tools for oil rigs and mines, and long-lasting springs.
Be.chemistry: Be²⁺ is so small that its compounds are largely **covalent**. Beryllium chloride forms polymer chains, and beryllium hydride is electron-deficient. The metal is protected by a thin oxide layer and does not react with water. Its oxide and hydroxide are **amphoteric**, dissolving in both acids and strong bases, which is another diagonal resemblance, this time to aluminium.

reactions.note: Reacts with acids once the oxide layer is removed.
Amphoteric: also dissolves in strong alkali, forming the beryllate ion.
Powdered beryllium burns brilliantly when heated.
Chadwick’s 1932 discovery of the neutron.

Be.safety: Beryllium is one of the most **toxic** non-radioactive elements when inhaled. Breathing its dust or fumes can cause **chronic beryllium disease** (berylliosis), an incurable lung disease, and beryllium is a known human carcinogen. Solid pieces are safe to touch, but machining is done with strict dust control.

B.history: Borax, a boron mineral, has been used for over a thousand years as a flux for gold-working and glazes. It was traded along the Silk Road from Tibet. The element was isolated in **1808**, almost at the same time, by **Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac** and **Louis Jacques Thénard** in Paris and by **Humphry Davy** in London. Both heated boric acid with potassium, but their product was only about 60 % pure. Truly pure boron was not prepared until 1909, by the American chemist Ezekiel Weintraub. The name combines *borax* (from Arabic and Persian) with the ending of *carbon*, which it resembles in some ways.
B.production:
The main ores are **borax** and **kernite** (sodium borates), together with colemanite and ulexite. **Turkey** has about 70 % of the world’s reserves, mined by the state company Eti Maden, and there are large deposits at the town of Boron, California. Most boron is sold as borates and boric acid. Impure amorphous boron is made by reducing boron oxide with magnesium (B₂O₃ + 3Mg → 2B + 3MgO). Very pure boron for electronics is made by reducing boron trichloride with hydrogen on hot filaments.

Uses include **borosilicate glass** (Pyrex) and glass-fibre insulation, ceramics, detergents, **neodymium magnets** (Nd₂Fe₁₄B), **boron carbide** armour, and neutron absorbers in nuclear reactors, since boron-10 captures neutrons strongly. Tiny amounts dope silicon to make p-type semiconductors.
B.chemistry: Boron is a **metalloid**, and the only non-metal in group 13. With only three valence electrons it forms **electron-deficient** compounds. BF₃ is a classic **Lewis acid** that accepts an electron pair, and the boron hydrides (boranes such as B₂H₆) contain unusual **three-centre two-electron bonds**: a hydrogen bridges two boron atoms with a single shared pair (William Lipscomb, Nobel Prize 1976). Elemental boron is extremely hard, and forms complex structures built from B₁₂ icosahedra.

reactions.note: Boron burns with a green flame.
Making amorphous boron (Moissan process).
A textbook Lewis acid–base adduct: nitrogen donates its lone pair to electron-deficient boron.
Making boric acid from borax.
Boric acid is a weak acid because it accepts OH⁻, rather than donating H⁺ directly.

B.safety: Elemental boron has low toxicity. Boric acid and borax are harmful if swallowed in quantity, and the EU classifies them as reproductive toxins. **Diborane** (B₂H₆) gas is very toxic and catches fire spontaneously in air.

C.history:
Carbon has been known since prehistory as charcoal, soot and lampblack, and diamonds were mined in India more than 2000 years ago. Its identity as an element came later. In **1772 Antoine Lavoisier** burned a diamond in a sealed jar using sunlight focused through a large lens, and found that it produced only carbon dioxide, the same as charcoal. In 1779 Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed that graphite is also carbon. Lavoisier listed carbon as an element in 1789, naming it after the Latin *carbo*, charcoal.

New forms of carbon are still being found. The football-shaped **buckminsterfullerene** C₆₀ was discovered in 1985 by Harold Kroto, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley (Nobel Prize 1996). Carbon nanotubes became famous in 1991. Single-atom-thick **graphene** was isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov using sticky tape (Nobel Prize 2010).
C.production: Carbon is mined as **coal** and **graphite** (mainly in China). **Coke**, made by heating coal without air, is the reducing agent in blast furnaces. **Synthetic graphite** is made by heating petroleum coke to about 3000 °C (the Acheson process) and is used for electrodes and battery anodes. **Synthetic diamonds** have been made since 1954, first by high-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) methods and now also by chemical vapour deposition (CVD), and they dominate industrial use. **Carbon black**, from burning heavy oil with limited air, makes tyres black and strong.
C.chemistry: Carbon forms four strong covalent bonds and links to itself in chains and rings of almost any length (**catenation**). This is why there are millions of organic compounds, and why life is carbon-based. Its allotropes have very different properties: **diamond** is the hardest natural material and an electrical insulator, while **graphite** is soft, slippery and conducts electricity along its layers. Carbon cycles through the atmosphere as CO₂, the main greenhouse gas from human activity. The radioactive isotope ¹⁴C (half-life 5730 years) is used for **radiocarbon dating**.

reactions.note: Complete combustion (ΔH = −394 kJ/mol).
Incomplete combustion in limited oxygen gives poisonous carbon monoxide.
In the blast furnace, CO from coke reduces iron ore to iron.
Steam over white-hot coke gives ‘water gas’, an old industrial fuel.
Thermal decomposition of limestone to quicklime.

C.safety: Elemental carbon has low toxicity, but fine dusts are hazardous. Coal dust causes ‘black lung’, carbon black is a possible carcinogen, and coal dust can explode in mines. Its oxides are the main hazards: **carbon monoxide** binds to haemoglobin and is a silent killer, and high CO₂ concentrations cause suffocation.

N.history: Nitrogen was discovered in **1772** by the Scottish physician **Daniel Rutherford**, a student of Joseph Black. He kept a mouse in a sealed container until it died, burned a candle in the remaining air, then removed the carbon dioxide. The gas left over, which he called ‘noxious air’, could support neither life nor flame. Carl Wilhelm Scheele, Henry Cavendish and Joseph Priestley studied it at about the same time. Lavoisier called it *azote* (‘without life’), still the French name. The English name comes from *nitrogène* (Jean-Antoine Chaptal, 1790), meaning ‘nitre-former’, because it is found in nitre (potassium nitrate, saltpetre).
N.production:
Air is 78 % nitrogen, so it is produced by **fractional distillation of liquid air** (N₂ boils at −196 °C, O₂ at −183 °C). Smaller supplies come from pressure-swing adsorption and membrane separators. The most important industrial reaction in history is arguably the **Haber–Bosch process** (Fritz Haber 1909, scaled up by Carl Bosch 1913). It converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia for fertilisers, and about half the world’s population is fed by crops grown with this synthetic nitrogen.

Nitrogen gas is used to blanket reactive chemicals and food packaging (it stops oxidation). Liquid nitrogen is used for freezing biological samples, and in cooking and dermatology.
N.chemistry: The N≡N **triple bond** is one of the strongest chemical bonds (945 kJ/mol), so nitrogen gas is very unreactive. Nature ‘fixes’ nitrogen through lightning and through the nitrogenase enzymes of bacteria, for example in the root nodules of legumes. Once fixed, nitrogen shows oxidation states from −3 (ammonia, NH₃) to +5 (nitric acid, HNO₃). Nitrogen is essential to life: it is in every amino acid, protein and DNA base.

reactions.note: Haber–Bosch: ΔH = −92 kJ/mol; iron catalyst, ~450 °C, ~200 atm (a compromise between rate and equilibrium yield).
Ostwald process step 1, on a platinum–rhodium gauze. It leads to nitric acid.
Absorbing nitrogen dioxide in water gives nitric acid.
The two gases meet and make a white smoke of ammonium chloride.
Happens in lightning and hot car engines; the source of NOₓ air pollution.

N.safety: Nitrogen is non-toxic, but it is a silent **asphyxiant**. In an enclosed space it displaces oxygen without any smell or warning, and people lose consciousness within seconds. **Liquid nitrogen** (−196 °C) causes severe cold burns. It expands about 700-fold on boiling, so it must never be sealed in a closed container. Divers breathing compressed air can suffer nitrogen narcosis, and ‘the bends’ if they surface too quickly.

O.history:
Oxygen was discovered independently by **Carl Wilhelm Scheele** in Uppsala (about **1771–72**, by heating mercury oxide and nitrates; he called it ‘fire air’) and by **Joseph Priestley** in England (**1774**, by focusing sunlight onto mercury oxide). Priestley published first, in 1775. Scheele’s book appeared in 1777. Priestley called the gas ‘dephlogisticated air’, still believing the old theory that burning releases a substance called phlogiston.

**Antoine Lavoisier** realised that combustion and rusting are reactions *with* this gas, which overturned the phlogiston theory and founded modern chemistry. In 1777 he named it *oxygène*, from Greek for ‘acid-former’, because he wrongly believed all acids contain oxygen. Hydrochloric acid does not.
O.production: Industrial oxygen is made by the **cryogenic fractional distillation of liquid air**, often over 100 million tonnes a year worldwide. Hospitals and home oxygen concentrators use **pressure-swing adsorption**, where zeolites absorb nitrogen. In the laboratory, oxygen is made by decomposing hydrogen peroxide with a manganese(IV) oxide catalyst. The biggest use is **steelmaking**: blowing pure oxygen through molten iron burns off excess carbon. Other uses include medicine, oxy-acetylene welding, liquid oxygen (LOX) as rocket oxidiser, and water treatment.
O.chemistry: Oxygen is the **most abundant element in Earth’s crust** (about 46 % by mass) and makes up 21 % of the air, all of it originally produced by photosynthesis. It is the second most electronegative element and forms oxides with almost every other element. O₂ is **paramagnetic**: liquid oxygen is pale blue and sticks between the poles of a magnet. This is explained by molecular orbital theory, which gives O₂ two unpaired electrons. Its other allotrope, **ozone** (O₃), forms the stratospheric layer that absorbs harmful UV light.

reactions.note: Combustion of natural gas.
MnO₂ catalyst: the standard laboratory preparation.
Cellular respiration releases the energy in food (the reverse of photosynthesis).
UV light or an electric discharge makes ozone.
Rusting needs both oxygen and water.

O.safety: Oxygen does not burn, but it makes other things burn far more fiercely. In oxygen-enriched air even ‘non-flammable’ materials can ignite. The **Apollo 1** crew died in 1967 in a cabin fire in pure oxygen. Oil or grease on high-pressure oxygen fittings can explode. Breathing oxygen at high partial pressure (for example in deep diving) is toxic to the nervous system and lungs.

F.history:
The mineral **fluorite** (CaF₂) was described in 1529 by Georgius Agricola as a flux that helps ores melt. The name comes from the Latin *fluere*, to flow. In 1771 Carl Wilhelm Scheele made **hydrofluoric acid**, which etches glass. Isolating the element itself proved deadly. Over the 19th century several chemists, the ‘fluorine martyrs’, were badly injured or killed by HF and fluorine, including the Irish Knox brothers and Paulin Louyet.

In **1886 Henri Moissan** finally succeeded by electrolysing potassium hydrogen fluoride dissolved in anhydrous HF at −50 °C, in an apparatus made of platinum–iridium with fluorite stoppers. He won the Nobel Prize in 1906. Large-scale production began in the 1940s for the Manhattan Project, which needed uranium hexafluoride (UF₆) to separate uranium isotopes.
F.production: Fluorine starts as fluorite. Treating it with sulfuric acid gives hydrogen fluoride (CaF₂ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + 2HF). Fluorine gas is then made by **electrolysis of a molten KF·2HF mixture** at about 100 °C, with carbon anodes and steel cathodes. Because the gas is so dangerous, it is usually made where it is used. Its main uses are **UF₆** for uranium enrichment, **SF₆** for electrical insulation, and fluorinated polymers. Fluoride compounds are used in toothpaste (NaF, SnF₂) and in about one in five pharmaceuticals. **PTFE** (Teflon), discovered by accident by Roy Plunkett in 1938, is also a fluorine compound.
F.chemistry: Fluorine is the **most electronegative element** (3.98) and the most reactive non-metal. It reacts, often violently, with almost everything except helium, neon and argon, and even forms compounds with xenon and krypton. Two factors explain this. The F–F bond is unusually **weak** (158 kJ/mol), because the lone pairs on the two small atoms repel each other. Bonds from fluorine to other elements are very **strong**. In compounds fluorine is always −1. The C–F bond is so strong that perfluorinated chemicals (PFAS) persist in the environment for a very long time.

reactions.note: Explodes even in the dark and at low temperature.
Fluorine can force even a noble gas to react (Neil Bartlett’s discoveries, 1962).
Fluorine oxidises water itself to oxygen.
Why hydrofluoric acid etches glass.
Making hydrogen fluoride from fluorite.

F.safety: Fluorine gas is **extremely toxic and corrosive**, and ignites many materials on contact. **Hydrofluoric acid** is especially treacherous: it may not hurt at first, but it soaks through the skin and attacks deep tissue and bone. It binds the body’s calcium, which can stop the heart. Calcium gluconate gel is the first-aid antidote. Fluoride in toothpaste is safe at the low doses used.

Ne.history:
Neon was discovered in **1898** at University College London by **William Ramsay** and **Morris Travers**. They had just found krypton by slowly boiling liquefied air. Next they examined the most volatile fraction of argon, and in an electric discharge it gave off a brilliant crimson-red glow. Travers later wrote that ‘the blaze of crimson light from the tube told its own story’. Ramsay’s 13-year-old son suggested the Latin *novum* (new), which became the Greek form *neon*.

In 1910 the French engineer **Georges Claude** made neon lamps, and in 1912 the first neon advertising sign appeared in Paris. Neon signs reached the United States in 1923, at a Packard car dealership in Los Angeles.
Ne.production: Neon is only 18 parts per million of the atmosphere, and is recovered as a by-product of large **air-separation plants**. A major part of the world’s high-purity neon for the semiconductor industry came from **Ukraine** (Odesa and Mariupol), so the 2022 war caused a worldwide shortage. Neon is used in **excimer lasers** (ArF and KrF) for printing computer chips, in helium–neon lasers (632.8 nm red light), as a cryogenic refrigerant (it boils at 27 K), and in the classic red-orange neon signs. Other ‘neon’ colours actually come from other gases or from coloured phosphor coatings.
Ne.chemistry: Neon has a full 2s²2p⁶ shell and a very high ionization energy (2081 kJ/mol). It forms **no stable chemical compounds**, making it arguably the least reactive of all elements, even less reactive than helium in some predictions. Only charged species such as NeH⁺ and NeAr⁺ have been seen fleetingly, in gas discharges and mass spectrometers.

reactions.eq: Ne + electrical energy → Ne* → Ne + red light
reactions.note: Neon does not react chemically. In a discharge tube, collisions excite its electrons, and their return to lower levels gives the famous red-orange glow (strongest lines 585–703 nm).

Ne.safety: Neon is non-toxic and non-flammable, but like any inert gas it can cause suffocation in a closed space. Liquid neon causes cold burns.
